title: PICC Placement
summary: PICC placement guidance for prolonged IV therapy, TPN or irritant/vesicant infusions, poor peripheral access, frequent blood draws, and reliable intermediate- to long-term central venous access.
provenance: Imported from procedure orders PDF updated 4.15.26
reviewNotes: Confirm low bleeding risk classification with local policy.
Confirm anticoagulation hold language with the final table.
Confirm dialysis access planning restrictions and escalation workflow.
Confirm whether BP control should remain in the PICC checklist.
Confirm outpatient AVS and discharge workflow.

items: Prolonged IV therapy, such as antibiotics or chemotherapy.
TPN or other irritant/vesicant infusions.
Poor peripheral venous access.
Frequent blood draws or recurrent IV medication administration.
Need for reliable intermediate- to long-term central venous access.
Low bleeding risk.
Warfarin: no holding requirement.
Heparin: no holding requirement.
Lovenox: no holding requirement.
DOACs: no holding requirement.
Plavix: no holding requirement.
Aspirin: no holding requirement.
Platelets >20k.

blocks.text: Procedure-specific pre-procedure orders have not yet been documented in this guide.

items: Local.
Confirm location.
Confirm duration and number of lumens.
DO NOT place in arm with AV fistula/graft or dialysis plan.
Review imaging with any prior axillary surgery or lymphedema.
Labs are appropriate.
Blood pressure is under control.
Confirm sedation plan - patient can lie flat.
assess the basilic, paired brachial, and cephalic veins; choose a patent vein large enough for the smallest suitable catheter.
brachial veins travel close to the brachial artery and median nerve; identify all three before puncture.
the catheter passes through the axillary, subclavian, and brachiocephalic veins into the SVC.
the lower SVC or cavoatrial junction provides high flow without placing the tip deep in the heart.
protect potential dialysis-access veins and avoid an arm with an AV access, active lymphedema, or significant venous obstruction.
indication, duration, required lumens, catheter size, and preferred arm.
use ultrasound to confirm patency, size, depth, and separation from the artery and nerve.
maintain maximal sterile technique and anesthetize the selected site.
puncture with real-time ultrasound, pass the wire gently, and confirm its central course.
measure the required length and guide the catheter centrally with fluoroscopy, ECG, or approved tip-navigation technology.
verify lower-SVC/cavoatrial position, then aspirate and flush every lumen.
apply the stabilization device and sterile dressing; record vein, length, tip position, and readiness for use.
identify the brachial artery and median nerve before access; stop for arterial blood, severe pain, or paresthesia.
use the smallest adequate catheter in a sufficiently large vein and avoid unnecessary lumens.
check for internal-jugular, contralateral, azygos, or high-SVC placement before clearing the line.
ectopy during advancement suggests right-atrial or ventricular entry; withdraw and reconfirm position.
avoid arms needed for dialysis access and reconsider placement with severe swelling, thrombosis, or central stenosis.
use maximal sterile barriers, secure without tension, and document the external length for later comparison.
